statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.

$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

derivations.claim:
Since $U$ is unitary, $U^{\otimes n}$ is unitary on the completed tensor
power by its isometric action on elementary tensors and its inverse
$(U^{-1})^{\otimes n}$. It commutes with every tensor-factor permutation,
because both compositions send an elementary tensor to
$Uh_{\pi(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Uh_{\pi(n)}$. It therefore commutes with the
symmetric averaging projection of [F2] and restricts to a unitary
$U_s^{(n)}$ on its range. The zeroth sector is the identity on $\mathbb C$.

The direct sum of the sector unitaries preserves the sum of squared
sector norms and has inverse $\bigoplus_n(U^{-1})_s^{(n)}$, so it is unitary.
It fixes the zeroth-sector vacuum and preserves finite sums of sectors in
both directions. On an elementary symmetric tensor, applying the Fock
creation formula before or after this direct sum gives the symmetrization of
$Uh$ together with the images of the original tensor factors; hence the two
creation maps intertwine. The annihilation formula is its adjoint contraction
and the same tensor calculation replaces each contracted vector $h$ by $Uh$.
Linearity, boundedness on each fixed sector, and density of elementary
tensors extend both identities to $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$.

Fix $n$. For an elementary tensor,
$$\|U_g^{\otimes n}(h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_n) -U_{g_0}^{\otimes n}(h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_n)\| \le\sum_{r=1}^n\prod_{s\ne r}\|h_s\|\, \|(U_g-U_{g_0})h_r\|,$$
by the telescoping expansion of the tensor difference and unitary norm
preservation. Strong continuity of $U_g$ makes the right side tend to zero.
Density of elementary tensors and the uniform norm bound $1$ extend
continuity to the completed sector and its closed symmetric subspace. Finite
sector sums are dense by [F1]; approximating an arbitrary Fock vector by
such a sum and using $\|\Gamma_s(U_g)\|=1$ proves strong continuity on the
whole direct sum.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

$\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ is the Schwartz space of smooth complex functions
whose coordinate-weighted derivatives are all bounded, as defined in
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].
Fix an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space and an inertial coordinate
chart as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use coordinates
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$ and metric $\eta=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, matching the
$(-+++)$ convention of the SR suppliers. Some QFT sources use its negative
$(+---)$; the Lorentz group is unchanged, and the phase is fixed explicitly
below.

Fourier phase below is dimensionless. A parameter $\mu\ge0$ has inverse-length
units and is only a mathematical shell parameter; it is not identified with a
physical rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, set
$$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2},\qquad
p_\mu(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k).$$
The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$

parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is
$$p\circ x:=p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))=
\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad
H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$

$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x.$$

\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x^0\xi^0+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\xi)}\,d^4x$ denotes
the standard transform in

=\widehat f\!\left(-\frac{p^0}{2\pi},\frac{\mathbf p}{2\pi}\right).$$

$$f(x)=(2\pi)^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R^4}
\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}
\,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$

Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.

$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

In the chart $\mathbf k\mapsto p_\mu(\mathbf k)$, write
$w_\mu(\mathbf k)=[2(2\pi)^3\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)]^{-1}$. Multiplication by
$\sqrt{w_\mu}$ is an isometry from $H_\mu$ onto
$L^2(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\},d^3\mathbf k)$ (for $\mu=0$) or
$L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k)$ (for $\mu>0$), with inverse division by
$\sqrt{w_\mu}$; the omitted point is Lebesgue-null. The full $L^2(\mathbb
R^3)$ is separable by [F1]. In the massless case extend any function on the
punctured space by zero at the null point, approximate it by the countable
dense family from [F1], and restrict those approximants back to the punctured
space; restriction does not increase the norm. Thus both chart spaces, and
therefore $H_\mu$, are separable.

Let $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$ for $\mu>0$ and
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ for $\mu=0$. For
$\Omega_n=\{1/n<|\mathbf k|<n\}$, these sets increase to $\Omega\setminus\{0\}$; its complement in $\Omega$ is null for the shell measure.
For $h\in L^2(\Omega,w_\mu d^3\mathbf k)$, monotone convergence [F5]
shows $\|h\mathbf1_{\Omega\setminus\Omega_n}\|_{L^2(w_\mu)}\to0$.
On each $\Omega_n$, $w_\mu$ is smooth and bounded above and below by
positive constants. Approximate $h|_{\Omega_n}$ in ordinary $L^2(\Omega_n)$
by a function in $C_c^\infty(\Omega_n)$ using [F2]; equivalence of the
weighted and ordinary norms on $\Omega_n$ gives weighted approximation.
Thus $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is dense in the shell space.

Fix $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Choose $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$
with $\rho(0)=1$, using [F4], and put
$$G(q^0,\mathbf q)= \psi(\mathbf q)\rho(q^0-\omega_\mu(\mathbf q)).$$
Because $\psi$ has compact support away from the massless apex, $\omega_\mu$
is smooth on a neighborhood of its support, so this is a smooth compactly
supported function on $\mathbb R^4$. By the Fourier automorphism [F3] there
is $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ with
$\mathcal F_+f(q^0,\mathbf q)=G(q^0,\mathbf q)$ in the convention of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. On the shell,
$K_\mu f(p_\mu(\mathbf k))=G(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)
=\psi(\mathbf k)$. Hence the test restriction range contains
$C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, which is dense by 2.1.

\mathcal F_+f(p^0,\mathbf p)e^{-i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}
\,dp^0\,d^3\mathbf p.$$
Thus this convention is a time reflection and rescaling of the cited
Schwartz automorphism and has the stated reciprocal normalization.
The proper orthochronous Lorentz group consists of linear maps preserving
$\eta$, orientation and the chosen future cone. A Poincare map is
$x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$ with $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda$ in that group.

This is a mathematical free scalar one-particle construction. It adopts the
chosen coordinates, measure and Fourier convention; it asserts no experimental
observation, physical mass identification or measurement outcome.

Assume Countable Choice. For every $\mu\ge0$, the measure $d\nu_\mu$ of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] is locally finite and sigma-finite on $H_\mu^+$.
For every proper orthochronous Lorentz transformation $\Lambda$ and every
nonnegative Borel function $g$ on $H_\mu^+$,
$$\int_{H_\mu^+}g(\Lambda^{-1}p)\,d\nu_\mu(p)
=\int_{H_\mu^+}g(p)\,d\nu_\mu(p).$$
The claim applies off the omitted apex when $\mu=0$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. For every $\mu\ge0$, the
space $H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu)$ of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] is separable, and
$$\{K_\mu f:f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)\}$$
is dense in $H_\mu$. If $\mu>0$, the range contains every function in
$C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$; if $\mu=0$, it contains every function in
$C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ and $K$ be complex
Hilbert spaces and let $U:H\to K$ be unitary. The sector maps
$U^{\otimes n}$ restrict to unitaries $U_s^{(n)}:H_s^{(n)}\to K_s^{(n)}$;
their direct sum
$$\Gamma_s(U)=\bigoplus_{n=0}^\infty U_s^{(n)}$$
is unitary, maps vacuum to vacuum, and maps the finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}(H)$ onto $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}(K)$. It intertwines the
creation and annihilation maps:
$$\Gamma_s(U)a_H^\dagger(h)\Gamma_s(U)^{-1}=a_K^\dagger(Uh),\qquad \Gamma_s(U)a_H(h)\Gamma_s(U)^{-1}=a_K(Uh)$$
on the finite-particle domain. If $g\mapsto U_g$ is a strongly continuous
family of unitaries, then $g\mapsto\Gamma_s(U_g)$ is strongly continuous.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. For every $\mu\ge0$, the
pointwise restriction
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{ip\circ x}\,d^4x$$
of [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] maps $\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ continuously
and linearly into $H_\mu$. It also annihilates the Klein–Gordon test operator:
$$K_\mu\bigl((\partial_0^2-\Delta+\mu^2)f\bigr)=0
\qquad(f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)).$$
The coordinates are the fixed length coordinates of that definition and
$\mu$ has inverse-length units.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Use the proper
orthochronous Poincare group
$G=\mathbb R^4\rtimes SO^+(1,3)$ in the coordinates of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. For $g=(a,\Lambda)\in G$, define
$$f_g(x)=f(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a)),\qquad
[U_\mu(g)h](p)=e^{ip\circ a}h(\Lambda^{-1}p).$$
Then $f_g\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$, $U_\mu(g)$ is a well-defined unitary
on $H_\mu$, $g\mapsto U_\mu(g)$ is a strongly continuous representation, and
$$K_\mu f_g=U_\mu(g)K_\mu f
\qquad(f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)).$$
The group product convention is
$(a,\Lambda)(b,\Gamma)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda\Gamma)$.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$ and its tensor extension is the bounded map of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$.

(a) There is a unique bounded linear operator $S\otimes T: H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$ for all $u\in H$, $v\in K$, and it satisfies $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

(b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$.

(c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$.

(d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

derivations.claim:
Since $K_\mu f,K_\mu\overline f\in H_\mu$ by [F9], the field formula is
defined on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The first term $a(K_\mu\overline f)$ is
complex-linear in $f$ because complex conjugation is followed by the
conjugate-linear dependence of $a$; the second is linear because both
$a^\dagger$ and $K_\mu$ are linear. Both terms preserve $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
by [F1,F2]. For real $f$, the shell vectors coincide, so
$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f)
=\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$. It is symmetric on the common
finite-particle domain by [F2]. Substituting $h=\sqrt2K_\mu f$ and $k=\sqrt2K_\mu g$ into [F3]'s
Weyl relation gives the stated scalar phase, and its vacuum Gaussian gives
$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}$.

For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, [F10] gives the one-particle representation and
$U_\mu(g)K_\mu f=K_\mu f_g$. Since the affine action is real,
$U_\mu(g)K_\mu\overline f=K_\mu\overline{f_g}$. The Fock lift [F7]
intertwines creation and annihilation, so the field formula in step 1.1 gives
$$\Gamma_s(U_\mu(g))\Phi_\mu(f)\Gamma_s(U_\mu(g))^{-1} =\Phi_\mu(f_g)$$
on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The explicit Segal Weyl formula [F3] and the same
lift give bounded Weyl covariance. Strong continuity of the Fock lifts
follows from [F7] and [F10].

Since $a(K_\mu\overline f)\Omega=0$ and
$\langle\Omega,a^\dagger(h)\Psi\rangle_2=0$, the vacuum one-point function
vanishes. Expanding the two fields, only
$a(K_\mu\overline f)a^\dagger(K_\mu g)\Omega$ contributes to the vacuum
pairing; CCR [F2] makes that value
$\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2$. Taking the first test to be $\overline f$ and the second $f$ gives $\|K_\mu f\|^2\ge0$; for real $f$ this is the ordinary diagonal. For an ordered product of $n$ real smeared fields,
write the first field as creation plus annihilation. The creation part
vanishes against the left vacuum; commute the annihilation part successively
past each later field using [F2]. Each commutator is the corresponding
two-point pairing, and the remaining annihilator kills the right vacuum.
This yields the recursive sum over its possible partner and proves the
Wick pairing rule by induction on $n$.

Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|C_h\|\le\|h\|$ for $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$. The tensor-extension bound and orthogonal symmetrizer in [F11] therefore give $\|a_n(h)\|\le\sqrt n\|h\|$ and $\|a_n^\dagger(h)\|\le\sqrt{n+1}\|h\|$, the latter also using $\|h\otimes v\|=\|h\|\|v\|$ from the product tensor pairing. Let $\Theta$ have sectors only through $N$. These bounds and orthogonality of distinct output sectors imply $\|\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\|\le(\sqrt N\|K_\mu\overline f\|+\sqrt{N+1}\|K_\mu f\|)\|\Theta\|$. Continuity of $K_\mu$ [F9] and conjugation [F12], followed by Hilbert Cauchy–Schwarz, makes every stated matrix coefficient continuous; complex linearity is step 1.1. Mutual adjoints [F2] give $\langle\Phi_\mu(f)\Psi,\Theta\rangle_2=\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for finite-particle vectors. Thus every such $\Theta$ lies in the adjoint domain with the asserted restricted adjoint action. Finite-particle invariance permits reversing every finite polynomial product by this identity, so for $\omega(B)=\langle\Omega,B\Omega\rangle_2$ one has $\omega(B^*B)=\|B\Omega\|^2\ge0$ and $\omega(I)=1$.

For a Schwartz test $\varphi(z)$, define $G_\varphi(p)=\int\varphi(z)e^{-ip\circ z}\,d^4z$; for $F(x,y)\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^8)$ define $G_F(p)=\int F(x,y)e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}\,d^4x\,d^4y$. By [F12], these are continuous Schwartz transforms, the second followed by the injective linear frequency restriction $L$ determined by the displayed phases. Injectivity in finite dimensions gives $|Lp|\ge c|p|$ for some $c>0$; each derivative of a restricted transform is a fixed finite linear combination of its ambient derivatives at $Lp$. These bounds control every weighted restricted derivative by finitely many ambient Schwartz seminorms, proving the claimed restriction continuity and decay. In either case $|G(p)|\le q_4(G)(1+|p|)^{-4}$, with $q_4$ a continuous Schwartz seminorm. The shell integral of $(1+|p|)^{-4}$ is finite by [F4]: its radial behavior is $O(r)$ at the massless apex, $O(r^2)$ near zero when $\mu>0$, and $O(r^{-3})$ at infinity. Therefore the integrals of $G_\varphi$ and $G_F$ against $d\nu_\mu$ define continuous complex-linear tempered distributions. On product tests $F(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ the inner integral is $\overline{K_\mu\overline f(p)}K_\mu g(p)$; its shell integral is exactly the covariance from step 2.2. This proves the relative and bidistribution interfaces without assigning point operators.

The one-particle translation phase is
$e^{i(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)a^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)}$, so its real
generator vector is $\varpi(\mathbf k)=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$.
It is finite and measurable. The measure is sigma-finite by [F5], so [F8]
applies and gives the joint PVM and vacuum at zero. On an $n$-particle
sector the joint multiplier is $\sum_{r=1}^n
(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k_r),-\mathbf k_r)$. Since
$|\sum_r\mathbf k_r|\le\sum_r|\mathbf k_r|\le\sum_r\omega_\mu(\mathbf k_r)$,
every such value lies in the closed future cone; the vacuum value does too.
Thus the joint spectral measure is supported there, as claimed.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. Tensoriality of $R$ is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a).
Lowering its output slot with the smooth metric and contracting with the
smooth inverse metric are intrinsic tensor operations
([[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] clauses (b)-(c),
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]]). Thus these formulas give smooth
fields of types $(0,4)$, $(0,2)$, $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$, respectively,
independent of the chart. Symmetry of $\operatorname{Ric}$ and $G$ is proved
separately in [[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clause (d).

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], with the curvature convention and tensors of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Let $\Omega:M\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth and dimensionless, and put $\widetilde g=\Omega^2g$ with the same orientation. Use the metric-selected connection and its tensor derivative of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Define the smooth one-form and its contractions by

$$u:=\Omega^{-1}d\Omega,\qquad H_{ab}:=(\nabla_a u)_b,\qquad \theta:=g^{ab}H_{ab},\qquad s:=g^{ab}u_au_b.$$

Then $H_{ab}=H_{ba}$ and

$$\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-2H_{ab}-g_{ab}\theta+2u_au_b-2g_{ab}s,$$

$$\widetilde S=\Omega^{-2}(S-6\theta-6s),$$

$$\widetilde G_{ab}=G_{ab}-2H_{ab}+2u_au_b+2g_{ab}\theta+g_{ab}s.$$

All curvature conventions are those stated in [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. These are mathematical transformation identities, not an assertion that the Einstein equation is conformally invariant.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let
$H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form
$\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$
This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric
and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is

$$K_0(\Box_\eta\psi)(p)=\int\psi(x)(-\partial_0^2+\Delta)e^{i(|\mathbf k|x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x=(\omega_0(\mathbf k)^2-|\mathbf k|^2)K_0\psi(p)=0,$$
and the same holds for $\overline\psi$ because $\Box_\eta$ has real coefficients. The field formula [F4] therefore gives $\Phi_0(\Box_\eta\psi)=a(K_0\Box_\eta\overline\psi)+a^\dagger(K_0\Box_\eta\psi)=0$. Taking $\psi=\Omega f$ proves $\Phi_g(P_gf)=0$. The operator $P_g$ preserves compact smooth tests because its coefficients are smooth.
